challenge: The overhead question is put as angels against the current outreach. The founders' hours could instead be treated as a shared limited budget across all routes, in which case the comparison is about where each hour is likely to produce the most.
challenge: People deciding how much a small early raise helps often look at the amount alone. A small sum extends the runway only if it is large compared with monthly spending, and the size of that sum compared with spending is not stated.
challenge: Hours pulled from main pipeline. If the founders' hours are fixed, time spent courting angels comes out of follow-up with the £1-2 million firms, which could slow the route most likely to bring the larger sum.
challenge: Short runway weakens negotiating position. If investors learn that cash is close to running out, they may slow down or ask for tougher terms, because they know the founders have little time to walk away.
challenge: Grant timelines outlast the runway. Grants often have fixed application windows and assessment periods, so if the one chosen has a decision date later than the cash-out date, the money may not arrive in time to help.
challenge: Widened targeting brings poorly fitting investors. Smaller-cheque or non-UK investors may need more explanation of the business or different legal paperwork, which could raise the founder hours needed per conversation without raising the chance of a commitment.

I want to explore alternatives to support the funding process

The aim is stated as securing funding, but the pressure comes from the cash running out. Anything that lengthens the runway, such as lower spending or non-dilutive money, may ease that pressure without closing a round in two months. Whether the two-month limit is a hard deadline or a proxy for runway is not stated.

Angel money is described as quicker, but how much quicker depends on whether angels who fit the business can be found, and on how much diligence they require. If it takes similar time to an institutional deal, the saving could be small.

The overhead question is put as angels against the current outreach. The founders' hours could instead be treated as a shared limited budget across all routes, in which case the comparison is about where each hour is likely to produce the most.

The current focus on UK firms doing £1-2 million deals may be what is slowing progress, or the slowness may come from the quality of introductions or the pitch. If it is the latter, more outreach to any investor group would meet the same result.

People deciding how much a small early raise helps often look at the amount alone. A small sum extends the runway only if it is large compared with monthly spending, and the size of that sum compared with spending is not stated.
Angel round complicates later terms. Early small investments can bring terms or shareholder expectations that some larger investors want to review, which could slow or deter later conversations.
Angel talks drag on. If angel conversations take as long as institutional ones, the quicker small sum may not arrive in time to be worth the founder hours spent.
Spending cuts weaken the pitch. If the cuts fall on things that show progress to investors, such as product work or sales, they could reduce the traction that investors look for.
Bridging loan adds repayment pressure. A loan has to be repaid, so if no larger funding follows, repayments could shorten the runway again after the initial extension.
